One of the oldest demonstrations comes from shadows. More than two thousand years ago, Eratosthenes compared the angle of shadows cast by vertical sticks in two Egyptian cities at the same time of day. Because the shadow angles differed, he concluded that the ground beneath the cities could not be flat. By combining the difference in angle with the distance between the cities, he estimated Earth’s circumference with surprising accuracy. The same experiment can be reproduced today with simple tools, communication between observers, and basic geometry.

The sky also provides evidence. Different stars are visible at different latitudes. Polaris, the North Star, rises higher above the horizon as an observer travels north and drops toward the horizon as the observer travels south. South of the equator, Polaris is not visible at all, while constellations such as the Southern Cross become prominent. A spherical Earth naturally explains these changing star fields: observers at different positions on a curved globe face different directions into space.

Lunar eclipses offer another clear example. During a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon. That shadow is consistently round. A flat disk would produce elongated or changing shadows at many angles, yet the observed shadow remains curved.

Modern navigation and communication systems reinforce the same conclusion. Long-distance flight paths often follow great-circle routes, which can appear curved on flat map projections but are the shortest paths on a globe. Satellite navigation, weather forecasting, global telecommunications, and Earth-observation imagery rely on orbital mechanics and spherical geometry.
